svg.title: Password encoding types compared: which are reversible, which survive an offline attack, and what to use in 2026
svg.desc: A table of six encoding types. Type 0 is cleartext - readable in the running configuration by anyone with a login. Type 4 is SHA-256 without iteration, rarely seen and not meaningfully better than type 5. Type 5 is salted MD5, which was acceptable in 2005 and now falls to commodity GPUs at billions of candidates per second, so an eight-character password is a matter of hours. Type 7 is a Vigenere-style obfuscation with a published key: it is reversible in one command, so a config backup containing type 7 is a plaintext password list with extra steps. Type 8 is PBKDF2-SHA256 with twenty thousand iterations. Type 9 is scrypt, memory-hard by design, and is the correct choice today because memory hardness is what defeats parallel hardware. A side panel shows the practical rule: enable secret with type 9, no type 7 anywhere, and a rotation plan for anything already stored as type 5. A footer notes that the encoding only buys time after a configuration file has already leaked - the first defence is that it should not leak.
svg.text: Type 7 is not encryption. It is a spelling of the password.
The only question that matters about an encoding is how long it survives after the config file is already in someone's hands.
zero - it is printed in show run
zero - a decoder is a web page
a plaintext list with extra steps
salted MD5, thousands of rounds at best
fast hash - cheap to brute force
rarely seen, no reason to choose
enable secret with type 9 on every device, no type 7 line surviving anywhere, and a dated migration for anything still stored as type 5.
Check it by search, not by memory: grep the running config for "password 7" and "secret 5" - the number of hits is the project size.
The honest caveat: hashing only buys time after the configuration has already leaked. Cleaning up the leak is the primary control; the encoding is the delay.
